hints: Use the substitution $u = 1 - \sin x$, so $\sin x = 1 - u$ and $\mathrm{d}u = -\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x$.
Express $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x\cos x$ to rewrite the integrand in terms of $u$.
Transform the limits: $x = \pi \implies u = 1$ and $x = \dfrac{3}{2}\pi \implies u = 2$.
walkthrough:
Given the substitution $u = 1 - \sin x$:
$$\sin x = 1 - u$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = -\cos x \implies \mathrm{d}u = -\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x \implies \cos x\,\mathrm{d}x = -\mathrm{d}u$$

Express the numerator $\sin(2x)$ using the double-angle identity:
$$\sin(2x) = 2\sin x\cos x$$
So the differential product becomes:
$$\sin(2x)\,\mathrm{d}x = 2\sin x(\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x) = 2(1 - u)(-\mathrm{d}u) = -2(1 - u)\,\mathrm{d}u = 2(u - 1)\,\mathrm{d}u$$

Transform the integration limits:
- Lower limit: when $x = \pi$, $u = 1 - \sin\pi = 1 - 0 = 1$
- Upper limit: when $x = \dfrac{3}{2}\pi$, $u = 1 - \sin\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\pi\right) = 1 - (-1) = 2$

Substitute into the integral:
$$\int_\pi^{\frac{3}{2}\pi} \dfrac{\sin(2x)}{\sqrt{1 - \sin x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_1^2 \dfrac{2(u - 1)}{\sqrt{u}}\,\mathrm{d}u = \int_1^2 2\left(\dfrac{u}{u^{1/2}} - \dfrac{1}{u^{1/2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u$$
$$= 2\int_1^2 (u^{1/2} - u^{-1/2})\,\mathrm{d}u$$

Integrate term by term using the power rule:
$$\int u^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}u = \dfrac{u^{3/2}}{3/2} = \dfrac{2}{3}u^{3/2}$$
$$\int u^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}u = \dfrac{u^{1/2}}{1/2} = 2u^{1/2}$$
Multiply by $2$:
$$2\left[ \dfrac{2}{3}u^{3/2} - 2u^{1/2} \right]_1^2 = \left[ \dfrac{4}{3}u^{3/2} - 4u^{1/2} \right]_1^2$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $u = 2$:
$$u^{3/2} = 2^{3/2} = 2\sqrt{2}, \quad u^{1/2} = \sqrt{2}$$
$$\text{Upper} = \dfrac{4}{3}(2\sqrt{2}) - 4\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{8\sqrt{2}}{3} - \dfrac{12\sqrt{2}}{3} = -\dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{2}$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $u = 1$:
$$u^{3/2} = 1, \quad u^{1/2} = 1$$
$$\text{Lower} = \dfrac{4}{3}(1) - 4(1) = \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{12}{3} = -\dfrac{8}{3}$$

Subtract the lower limit from the upper limit:
$$\text{Integral} = \text{Upper} - \text{Lower} = -\dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{2} - \left(-\dfrac{8}{3}\right) = \dfrac{8}{3} - \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{2}$$

State the final exact answer in the form $a + b\sqrt{2}$:
$$a = \dfrac{8}{3}, \quad b = -\dfrac{4}{3}$$
$$\dfrac{8}{3} - \dfrac{4}{3}\sqrt{2}$$
